catalog_quote: 2.3 Tone All P-zone languages are tonal (though Ndengereko is losing distinctive prosody under Swahili influence). In terms of tonal inventory, all languages restrict contour tones to heavy syllables, long vowels, and VN sequences in Yao and Mwera. ... Matuumbi allows LL (cháchaandųka ‘taste sour’), LH (mboópo ‘machete’) and HL (į́įmba ‘swell’), but generally avoids HH. ... There is attraction of final H to a long penult in Matuumbi (m#boópo ← m#boopó ‘machete’) and Yao (n-aa#páámbukwiíle ← n-aa#páámbukwiilé ‘I uncovered’). [sec. 2.1, p. 531] Matuumbi shortens vowels which are too far to the left in an utterance. At the word level, stem vowels are generally shortened before the antepenultimate mora, thus áand-įk-a ‘write’, ándįk-įy-a ‘make write’; tyátyaak-įy-a ‘plaster’, tyátyak-įy-įlw-a ‘be plastered’, káat-a ‘cut’, kát-an-įk-a ‘be cuttable’. With two long vowels, the first is shortened
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Matumbi (matu1259) is not in the catalog. The four title-hits are all about Kimatuumbi tone analysed through abstract accent/metrical structure (Odden 1982 WCCFL 1; Odden 1985 Benjamins pp. 345-420, doi:10.1075/ssls.6.18odd; Pulleyblank 1983 Foris/De Gruyter doi:10.1515/9783112420102-014) or a ~30-language East Bantu tone/accent typology (Philippson 1991 thesis, print/ANRT only; theses.fr abstract read). None could be opened: Benjamins, De Gruyter, OUP, ScienceDirect, HathiTrust and WorldCat all bot-blocked or paywalled; Unpaywall reports all closed; neither the 1983 Foris nor the 1985 Benjamins volume is on archive.org; WCCFL 1 is print-only. What was read (open): Odden's own manuscripts from his OSU homepage (Vowel Length, African Tone, Bantu Phonology) — Kimatuumbi has a mora-counting lexical tone system with contour tones only on long vowels; no stress statement. Secondary open text (Clements & Goldsmith 1984, archive.org scanned) and lending snippets (Odden 1988; Pulleyblank 1986) confirm that the 'accent' in these titles is a tonal/metrical accent governing H placement and vowel-length distribution (long vowels only in penult/antepenult, 'strong foot'), not word stress; Pulleyblank 1986 groups Kimatuumbi with 'stress or pitch accent languages'. The authoritative descriptions remain Odden 1996 (OUP grammar) and Odden 2026 'Matumbi Phonology' (Elsevier IELL), both paywalled and not in the item list. Priority for acquisition: Odden 1985 high (76-page accentual analysis), Pulleyblank 1983 and Odden 1982 medium (superseded by Odden 1985/1996), Philippson 1991 medium (Matumbi coverage unverified).fr, Sudoc, archive.org and the Internet Archive.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Matumbi is described as a tone language (H vs L, contours only on long vowels/heavy syllables, tense-determined verbal tone, final H attracted to a long penult); contrastive vowel length is confined to the last three moras of the word and to phrase heads. The source makes no statement about word stress or accent for Matumbi at all; no fixed stress position is described.
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress; for length, the first of two long stem vowels shortens, reduplicant penults keep length, phrase-head shortening before a modifier
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level and phrase-level tone and length; citation forms and phrasal forms both given. The absence of a stress statement in Odden's accessible descriptions (2003 sketch, 1980 tone paper, 2006 encyclopedia snippets, three later mss) is an absence, not a claim; the fuller descriptions (Odden 1996, 2026) were not accessible.
new_statements.identity_note: Odden's 'Kimatuumbi'/'Matuumbi' (Kipatimu area, Kilwa District, Guthrie P13) = Glottolog Matumbi matu1259 (ISO mgw). The quoted 2003 chapter uses Matuumbi as its representative of P10 and its general sentence covers 'all P-zone languages'; the Matuumbi-specific data come from Odden's own fieldwork (Odden 1996). Krumm 1912 spells the language Kimatumbi. No dialect is distinguished in any source seen.

[statut de la syllabe pénultième] : néant. »
new_statements.translation: (ch.5 §2) 'This is Matuumbi (group XIII), very well studied by Odden (forthcoming), on whom I draw heavily. Matuumbi is an accent language whose association rule at the lexical level is fairly unproblematic: roughly, a H associates to each marked syllable (only one per morpheme), with, in addition, in certain noun stems, an "echo" H appearing on the second mora of the stem.' (Annexe) '3: accentual language with H* melody; 8: an accent on the initial moves to the second mora, unless that is the final, in which case it is deleted; the H associates to each marked syllable; 9: a H on the final retracts to the second mora of a preceding long syllable; 10 [status of the penultimate syllable]: none.'

new_statements.relation_note: Type label differs: the catalog record (Odden 2003, 'All P-zone languages are tonal') files Matuumbi as tone language with a stress statement, whereas Philippson 1991 analyses the same H-tone facts as an ACCENTUAL (pitch accent) system with lexically placed accents realised as H ('langue accentuelle à mélodie H*'), explicitly after Odden's own earlier accentual analysis (Odden 1984 ms; Pulleyblank 1982), which Odden later abandoned for a privative H/toneless tonal analysis (Odden 1996; 2003; 2006 'H-toned versus toneless distinction'). On the facts the two sources agree and Philippson adds detail: retraction of a final H onto a long penult (= Odden 2003 'attraction of final H to a long penu…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Philippson (following Odden's 1984 ms 'An accentual approach to tone in Kimatuumbi' and Pulleyblank 1982) classifies Matuumbi as an accentual language ('langue à accent', 'langue accentuelle à mélodie H*'): surface H tones are the realisation of lexically/morphologically marked (accented) syllables, at most one mark per morpheme but possibly several H per word (ch.1 p.41: Matuumbi words may carry several 'accents' but every word has at least one, a default constituent being built). Accent position is lexical, not fixed: dissyllabic noun stems have 3 prosodic schemes (-cvcv, -c*vcv, -cvc*v); an accent on a word-initial mora shifts to the second mora or is deleted if that mora is final (ch.6 pp.438-439: 'le matuumbi a réorganisé le système tonal en système accentuel.. un accent lexical ne peut se manifester sur la première more d'un mot'); a final H retracts onto the second mora of a preceding long syllable; an all-L word gets a H on its second mora before absolute pause (p.312). The penultimate syllable has NO special status (annexe rubrique 10 'néant': no demarcative penultimate stress or lengthening), though the vowel-length contrast is realised only in penultimate or antepenultimate position, 'ce qui s'explique sans doute par des contraintes métriques (il s'agit de langues à accent)' (p.484), and a H on the penult also associates to the final before absolute pause (p.484). Phrase-level: vowel shortening and loss of perfective verbal H before a directly governed complement (ch.5 sec.2.1).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress discussed for Matuumbi; several H (accents) per word are possible, none singled out as primary; no penultimate demarcative accent ('10. : néant').
new_statements.exceptions: Accent cannot surface on a word-initial mora (shifts to 2nd mora, or deleted when the 2nd mora is final, e.g. lulémi vs ndemi y&aab&E); the cl.5 'prefix' lii- is a clitic and does not count for lexical accent placement; length neutralised before NC and after glides and lost when pushed left of the antepenult (k&aata / k&atanika); certain verb-focus tenses escape phrasal shortening; the stem -ana 'child' is unaccented in Matuumbi.
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson's Matuumbi data are Odden's (Kimatuumbi, P13, Kilwa district, Tanzania; sources listed p.518: Odden 1984 'An accentual approach to tone in Kimatuumbi', Odden ms. Yale 60 pp., Odden forthcoming 'Kimatuumbi phonology and morphology', Pulleyblank 1982 'Accent in Kimatuumbi'); no dialect distinguished.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement of TYPE LABEL, not of facts: the catalog (Odden 2003 in Nurse & Philippson, sec. 2.3) classes Matuumbi as tonal ('All P-zone languages are tonal') with H restricted patterns and final-H attraction to a long penult; Philippson 1991 (ch.5 sec.2, ch.6 sec.2.5.2, annexe p.506) classes Matuumbi as an accentual / pitch accent language ('langue à accent', 'langue accentuelle à mélodie H*') in which lexically marked syllables (one per morpheme, possibly several per word) receive H, initial accents shift to the second mora, and a final H retracts onto a long penult, with the penultimate otherwise having no special status ('néant'). Philippson follows Odden's own pre-1996 accentual analysis (Odden 1982, 1984/1985; Pulleyblank 1983), which Odden later recast as a privative H-vs-toneless tone system (1996, 2003, 2006). Both sources agree there is no fixed word-stress position and agree on the H-retraction and length-distribution facts; the difference is the 1980s accentual vs later tonal framing.
